# Product Minds on Wheels (PMW)

AI decision support for BMW product managers: from customer evidence to traceable, prioritised requirements for
the next vehicle generation, with the product manager deciding every step. EHL Grand Finale 2026, BMW track.

```
Customer voice → Signal → Root cause → Customer need → Requirement → Priority + Confidence → PM decision → Audit trail
```

## Run it (10 minutes)

Needs: Node 24, current npm, and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). The pipeline reads
the supplied PDFs directly with Python, including on Windows.

```bash
# 1. Build the database (about 10 seconds)
cd pipeline
uv sync
uv run pmw build --offline  # complete evidence drafts; no network generation
uv run pmw verify          # citations, counts and deterministic scoring checks
# uv sync --extra llm && ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... uv run pmw build --llm   # AI mode, see below

# 2. Run the web app
cd ../web
npm ci
npm run dev                 # http://localhost:3000
```

Rebuilding wipes the database, including every PM decision. That is the clean demo state.
After pulling changes to `pipeline/pmw/db.py`, rebuild: the build drops and recreates every table.

Equipment matches stay within the feature's allowed topics. Only `Wants` comments support option, package or
cross-vehicle offers; complaints about standard equipment are marked `standard_but_failing`.
Each vehicle keeps its 15 signal requirements plus up to five quick wins, ranked by distinct wishing comment IDs.
G60 and G70 also include their three strongest in-scope China/Europe survey conflicts, with explicit market values,
2025 sales shares and limited evidence confidence. These cards do not invent customer comments.
Quick wins name the feature and option/package code or source vehicle, and use their own comments and scores.
Comment IDs are the available counting unit; the source data does not identify unique people across comments.

Schema update: `equipment_matches.feature` identifies the feature; the placeholder `equipment.trim` column was
removed. Rebuild the database before running the updated app.

Phase 2 adds `signal_feedback` (full negative-comment membership for live approval coverage) and `feedback_scope`
(readable text exclusions). Rebuild before using this branch. The async `happiness(viewer, vehicle)` gate function
returns authorized markets only and `share: null` when evidence is missing; the meter UI can consume it.
Implementation notes: [Happiness data](docs/HAPPINESS_DATA.md), [survey and scope](docs/SURVEY_AND_SCOPE.md),
[photos](docs/REQUIREMENT_PHOTOS.md), and [pitch data traps](docs/pitch/data-traps.md).

Vishwa Phase 2 adds a region-aware evidence/assumption meter and `/portfolio`, a theme-by-vehicle heatmap with
aggregate counts only. The additive `requirements.evidence_mix` and `evidence_mix_by_market` columns can be
backfilled without replacing decisions: back up the existing database, then run `uv run pmw evidence-mix` from
`pipeline`. A full rebuild is still needed to regenerate upstream source changes. See the [Phase 2 delivery and
migration notes](docs/PHASE2_VISHWA.md) and [scoring pitch](docs/pitch/scoring.md).

Regression checks: `cd pipeline && uv run --extra llm python -m unittest discover -s tests -v`, then
`cd ../web && node --test scripts/test-equipment-evidence.mjs scripts/test-happiness.mjs scripts/test-score.mjs && npx tsc --noEmit && npm run build`.
Run `npm run test:e2e` after building; it uses a separate copy of the local database.

**Priority display:** the list is grouped MoSCoW-style by priority score: Must have 65+, Should have 55+, Could have 45+,
Won't have this time below 45 (`MOSCOW` in `web/components/ui.tsx`). The Act / Validate first / Monitor / Park chip is the
separate decision quadrant (priority × confidence).

**Priority weights and presets:** the "Priority weights" panel above the requirement list lets a product manager change
how much each of the five priority factors counts (customer impact, frequency, market relevance, competitive pressure,
future relevance), by slider or with a strategy preset: Customer first, Premium experience, Quick wins, China focus or
Europe focus (defined and explained in `web/lib/score.ts`). A live preview shows how the top 5 would re-order before
anything is saved. Apply needs a reason; the weights are stored team-wide in `settings.weights_active` and logged in the
audit trail (who, region, before/after, why). While they are active, every page and export recomputes priority with the
pipeline's formula, `round(100 × Σ weight·value / Σ weight)`, re-groups MoSCoW and re-derives the quadrant; confidence
is never changed because it measures evidence, not strategy. The stored scores stay untouched, so Reset restores the
original ranking exactly. `node --test scripts/test-score.mjs` proves the web formula reproduces every stored priority
and quadrant under the default weights.

## Hosted demo

Live at **https://product-minds-on-wheels.vercel.app** (Vercel project `product-minds-on-wheels`).

- Online, the app reads and writes a hosted Turso database (SQLite in the cloud, free plan, added through the
  Vercel Marketplace). Locally it uses `db/pmw.sqlite`. Same code, chosen in `web/lib/db.ts`.
- Update the hosted data after a pipeline change: `cd web && vercel env pull .env.local && npm run db:push`.
  This replaces everything online, including PM decisions made on the hosted demo.
- Deploy code: `cd web && vercel deploy --prod`. The project is not connected to GitHub, so pushes do not deploy.
- Search engines are kept out three ways (robots meta tag, `robots.txt`, `X-Robots-Tag` header). No analytics,
  and the font is self-hosted, so visitors' browsers make no requests to third parties.

## How it fits together

```
data/*.xlsx, *.PDF ─────► pipeline/ (Python) ──► db/pmw.sqlite ──► web/ (Next.js) ──► product manager
                              │                        ▲                 │
                              └── pipeline/cache/ ─────┘                 └── decisions + access events
                                  (AI drafts, committed)                     written back to audit_events
```

| Step | Where | Who does it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Ingest, record data problems | `pipeline/pmw/ingest.py` | AI pipeline, automatic |
| 2 Signals (themes from comments) | `pipeline/pmw/signals.py` | AI pipeline, automatic |
| 3 Triangulate (survey, sales, equipment, conflicts, missing voices) | `pipeline/pmw/evidence.py` | AI pipeline, automatic |
| Scope guard | `pipeline/pmw/scope.py` | AI pipeline, automatic, every exclusion has a reason |
| 4 Derive requirement (the ladder) | `pipeline/pmw/derive.py` | AI drafts, never final |
| 5 Priority and confidence | `pipeline/pmw/score.py` | Deterministic code, not the LLM |
| 6 Approve / validate first / edit / reject / challenge | `web/lib/actions.ts` | **Product manager, mandatory** |
| 7 Audit trail | `audit_events` table, `/audit` page | Automatic, append-only |

**Two rules that keep the system honest**
- Language comes from AI, numbers come from code. Scores are never written by the model.
- Priority and confidence are separate. High priority with weak evidence lands in **Validate first**, not **Act**.

## Regions instead of logins

There is no login. The region picker in the header (top right) sets a cookie. A market product manager sees raw
customer comments from their own market only; summary scores stay visible everywhere; the head of product
(All markets) sees everything. All reads go through `web/lib/gate.ts`, which filters by region and logs access.
In production this maps onto BMW single sign-on and database-level security.

## AI mode

`uv run pmw build --llm` classifies unlabelled feedback, drafts requirements and explains challenges.
Validated results are cached by their full inputs in `pipeline/cache/`; commit those files after a live run
so teammates can replay them without a key. Model: set `PMW_MODEL` (and optionally `PMW_MODEL_FAST`) in
`pipeline/.env`. `--offline` reads validated caches but prohibits network calls even if a key exists.
Without a matching cache, the pipeline uses explicit evidence-based templates and provisional rule labels.
Live-model caches are not included in the offline-first deliverable.

Implementation, checks and limitations: [Vishwa pipeline handoff](docs/VISHWA_IMPLEMENTATION.md).

Optional voice agent (OpenAI Realtime): [setup, tools and safety](docs/VOICE_COPILOT.md). Set the server-side `OPENAI_API_KEY` in `web/.env.local`, then click the small microphone at the bottom of any page to talk to PMW in English or German.

## Repo map

```
data/                BMW hackathon files
db/pmw.sqlite        built by the pipeline (git-ignored)
pipeline/pmw/        Python pipeline; db.py is the schema = the contract with the web app
pipeline/cache/      cached AI drafts (committed)
web/lib/gate.ts      every data read, region filtering, access logging
web/lib/actions.ts   every PM decision and its audit events
web/app/             pages: / (home), /vehicles/[code] (requirements, matrix, signals, data health), /audit
web/components/      UI; DecisionCard.tsx is the core screen
```

Team, ownership and workflow: [TEAM.md](TEAM.md).

**Note:** the repo contains BMW data and photography provided for the hackathon. Check the hackathon terms before keeping it public.

content.text:
Everything is in `main` and on the live site: **https://product-minds-on-wheels.vercel.app**

## What went live
**PR #22** (`0bc8b3a`) added:
- the top bar with **Board** and **Radar**
- the MoSCoW Requirements board, with Vishwa's **Decisions** board as a tab on each car page
- the Decision Card tabs, the evidence and assumptions meter and the "Why the AI recommends this" line
- Market-conflict flags and the compact Happiness Meter on the board
- **OpenAI voice**, set up to ignore background talk while it's speaking, with ElevenLabs as backup
- the new README

**PR #24** (`0a39f3f`): a privacy fix I found while checking the live site (next section).

I added the three voice keys to Vercel **Production** as sensitive variables, without printing them.

## Bug found during the check
The **China export contained 18 US customer comment IDs**, inside the root-cause text the pipeline writes. A China product manager could also see them on the Decision Card. This predates today's release; my earlier checks only looked at quotes and missed it. Comment IDs from markets you're not allowed to see are now replaced with "[comment from United States]" everywhere: the app, the board drawer, the exports and the voice agent. A new test checks it from a China viewer's point of view.

## Checked on the live site
- All pages load: home, car pages and their tabs, Board, Radar, Workflow, Audit trail and the export.
- Top bar, no sidebar; card tabs, evidence meter and mic are present.
- Live voice starts **OpenAI** sessions.
- China export: **0** comment IDs for both the 7 and 5 Series. The All-markets export still shows its 178.
- Still hidden from search engines.
- **55 / 55 browser tests** and **18 / 18 voice tests** pass.

## README
Rewritten in plain language for the current app:
- a tour of every page and tab
- how the work is split between the pipeline and the product manager
- regions instead of logins
- how to run, test and deploy
- the three voice modes and their settings
- where things live in the repo

I left out the old per-PR change notes and checked it for buzzwords and for any mention of Claude.

## Housekeeping
- Your main folder is on the latest `main`, and the voice keys are now in its gitignored `web/.env.local`, so `npm run dev` has working voice. The temporary work copy is removed.
- **PR #19 (Vishwa's `feature_v`) is still open.** #22 replaced it. Tell Vishwa before closing it, and ask him to branch from `main` from now on.
- **The live data has test traces:** 9 "latency test" voice entries in the audit trail. Run `cd web && npm run db:push` before the demo for a clean start. It also wipes any decisions made on the live site.
- **Rotate the OpenAI and ElevenLabs keys** after the hackathon.

Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

content.content:
Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit, and the commit carries an `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer linking the two.
**Checkpoint IDs** are 26-character ULIDs (e.g. `REDACTED`), which sort by creation time. Checkpoints written by older versions of Entire carry a legacy 12-character hex ID (e.g. `a3b2c4d5e6f7`); both formats stay readable in the same repo, and you can pass either to any command that takes a checkpoint ID.
### Checkpoint Storage
Checkpoints live in your repository's own git object store, never in your branch's history. Each checkpoint is its own git ref:
```
refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>
```
The ref points at a commit whose tree *is* that checkpoint — `metadata.json`, the per-session transcript files, and any subagent task records. `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID, which keeps the refs evenly distributed.
Because checkpoints are independent refs, they are written, pushed, and fetched independently. There is no shared branch tip for concurrent sessions to contend on, and a reader can fetch exactly the one checkpoint it needs instead of a whole history. A checkpoint written on another machine is fetched on demand the first time you read it.
`entire enable` sets this up; there is nothing to configure. It is recorded in `.entire/settings.json` as:
```json
{
  "checkpoints": {
    "primary": { "type": "git-refs" }
  }
}
```
Inspect what a repo has locally with plain git, or through Entire:
```bash
git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints    # the raw refs
entire checkpoint list                      # checkpoints on this branch
entire checkpoint explain <id>              # one checkpoint in full
```
### How It Works
```
Your Branch                      Checkpoint storage
     │                                  │
     ▼                                  │
[Base Commit]                           │
     │                                  │
     │  ┌─── Agent works ───┐           │
     │  │  Turn 1           │           │
     │  │  Turn 2           │           │
     │  │  Turn 3           │           │
     │  └───────────────────┘           │
     │                                  │
     ▼                                  ▼
[Your Commit] ─────────────────► [Checkpoint]
  Entire-Checkpoint: <id>          (transcript, prompts,
     │                              files touched, tokens)
     ▼
```
As you work, Entire tracks which files the agent touched (and their content hashes) in local session state, alongside a local copy of the transcript; nothing is written to git until you commit. When you commit, that work is condensed into a permanent checkpoint and linked to your commit by an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.
### Strategy
Entire uses a manual-commit strategy that keeps your git history clean:
- **No commits on your branch** — Entire never creates commits on the active branch
- **Safe on any branch** — works on main, master, and feature branches alike
- **Metadata stored separately** — session data lives in per-checkpoint refs, never in your branch's history
### Git Worktrees
Entire works seamlessly with [git worktrees](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree). Each worktree has independent session tracking, so you can run multiple AI sessions in different worktrees without conflicts.
### Concurrent Sessions
Multiple AI sessions can run on the same commit. If you start a second session while another has uncommitted work, Entire warns you and tracks them separately. Both sessions' checkpoints are preserved, and a commit condenses every session with pending work in that worktree.
## Headless & CI Authentication
By default `entire login` opens a browser to sign in and stores tokens in the OS keyring (macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service, Windows Credential Manager). Machines without a usable browser or keyring — headless servers, containers, minimal VMs, CI runners — have two supported paths:
### Interactive login on a headless machine
Sign-in itself already handles this: with no interactive terminal, over SSH, or on a Linux or BSD machine with no graphical display, `entire login` switches to the device-code flow on its own and prints an approval URL you can open on any machine. `entire login --device` forces that flow explicitly. Only token *storage* needs an override — use the file-backed store:
```bash
ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file entire login
```
Tokens are written with `0600` permissions to `tokens.json` in your Entire config directory (`~/.config/entire` by default). Override the location with `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH`. Set `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` persistently (e.g. in your shell profile) so later commands read from the same store.

Because checkpoints are independent refs, they are written, pushed, and fetched independently. There is no shared branch tip for concurrent sessions to contend on, and a reader can fetch exactly the one checkpoint it needs instead of a whole history. A checkpoint written on another machine is fetched on demand the first time you read it.
`entire enable` sets this up; there is nothing to configure. It is recorded in `.entire/settings.json` as:
```json
{
  "checkpoints": {
    "primary": { "type": "git-refs" }
  }
}
```
Inspect what a repo has locally with plain git, or through Entire:
```bash
git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints    # the raw refs
entire checkpoint list                      # checkpoints on this branch
entire checkpoint explain <id>              # one checkpoint in full
```
### How It Works
```
Your Branch                      Checkpoint storage
     │                                  │
     ▼                                  │
[Base Commit]                           │
     │                                  │
     │  ┌─── Agent works ───┐           │
     │  │  Turn 1           │           │
     │  │  Turn 2           │           │
     │  │  Turn 3           │           │
     │  └───────────────────┘           │
     │                                  │
     ▼                                  ▼
[Your Commit] ─────────────────► [Checkpoint]
  Entire-Checkpoint: <id>          (transcript, prompts,
     │                              files touched, tokens)
     ▼
```
As you work, Entire tracks which files the agent touched (and their content hashes) in local session state, alongside a local copy of the transcript; nothing is written to git until you commit. When you commit, that work is condensed into a permanent checkpoint and linked to your commit by an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.
### Strategy
Entire uses a manual-commit strategy that keeps your git history clean:
- **No commits on your branch** — Entire never creates commits on the active branch
- **Safe on any branch** — works on main, master, and feature branches alike
- **Metadata stored separately** — session data lives in per-checkpoint refs, never in your branch's history
### Git Worktrees
Entire works seamlessly with [git worktrees](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree). Each worktree has independent session tracking, so you can run multiple AI sessions in different worktrees without conflicts.
### Concurrent Sessions
Multiple AI sessions can run on the same commit. If you start a second session while another has uncommitted work, Entire warns you and tracks them separately. Both sessions' checkpoints are preserved, and a commit condenses every session with pending work in that worktree.
## Headless & CI Authentication
By default `entire login` opens a browser to sign in and stores tokens in the OS keyring (macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service, Windows Credential Manager). Machines without a usable browser or keyring — headless servers, containers, minimal VMs, CI runners — have two supported paths:
### Interactive login on a headless machine
Sign-in itself already handles this: with no interactive terminal, over SSH, or on a Linux or BSD machine with no graphical display, `entire login` switches to the device-code flow on its own and prints an approval URL you can open on any machine. `entire login --device` forces that flow explicitly. Only token *storage* needs an override — use the file-backed store:
```bash
ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file entire login
```
Tokens are written with `0600` permissions to `tokens.json` in your Entire config directory (`~/.config/entire` by default). Override the location with `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE_PATH`. Set `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file` persistently (e.g. in your shell profile) so later commands read from the same store.

The redaction described in this document applies identically to both — the pipeline is shared, and only the destination differs. Where the distinction matters below, it is called out.
20:Between commits, Entire writes nothing to git. At the end of each agent turn it records the paths the agent touched and their git blob hashes in local session state (`.git/entire-sessions/`), and keeps the sanitized transcript in `.entire/metadata/<session>/full.jsonl` (see [Persistence of un-redacted-by-OPF content](#persistence-of-un-redacted-by-opf-content)). Older Entire versions instead wrote local **shadow branches** (`entire/<commit>-<worktree>`) at turn end, whose code-file snapshots were raw, unredacted blobs of your working tree. Current versions do not delete them automatically: `entire doctor` reports them and `entire doctor --force` deletes the `entire/<commit>-<worktree>` form without touching session state. Plain `entire clean` deletes them too, but also clears the state of every session based on HEAD, which is now the only record of pending agent work. `entire disable --uninstall` deletes the `entire/<commit>-<worktree>` form as well, and lists the oldest `entire/<commit>` form by name without deleting it (a user's own branch named like a short SHA matches it); `entire clean --all` deletes that form after you confirm. Deleting a branch leaves its objects unreachable until git prunes them: `git gc` reclaims the space once they are two weeks old (git's default `gc.pruneExpire`). `git gc --prune=now` frees it at once but drops every unreachable object, recently dropped stashes included, and must only run when no other git process is active.
26:If your repository is **public**, this data is visible to the entire internet.
28:### What Entire redacts automatically
30:Entire automatically scans transcript and metadata content before writing it to a git object. Five always-on secret detection methods plus a configurable scanner layer (pattern matching, method 2 below) run during condensation, plus a conditional seventh pass for user-defined secret rules (see [Customizing redaction](#customizing-redaction) below), an opt-in eighth pass for PII (see [Optional PII redaction](#optional-pii-redaction) below), and an opt-in ninth pass that shells out to the OpenAI Privacy Filter model (see [Optional OpenAI Privacy Filter](#optional-openai-privacy-filter-opf) below):
32:1. **Entropy scoring** — Identifies high-entropy strings (Shannon entropy > 4.5) that look like randomly generated secrets, even if they don't match a known pattern. One exact shape is exempt from this layer only: a string that is, in its entirety, a Claude Code tool-use id (`toolu_01` plus 22 letters or digits). The other layers still scan it, and a secret attached to an id forms a longer string that is not exempt.
33:2. **Pattern matching** — Runs one or both configurable scanner engines against known secret formats: [Betterleaks](https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks) (default on) and/or [goredact](https://github.com/lastpersonlabs/goredact) (default off). See [Choosing secret-scanner engines](#choosing-secret-scanner-engines) below.
34:3. **Provider token prefixes** — Deterministically redacts known secret-key prefixes (e.g. Supabase `sb_secret_`, `sbp_`) regardless of entropy or surrounding context.
35:4. **Credentialed URI detection** — Redacts URLs with embedded passwords, such as `REDACTED`.
36:5. **Database connection-string detection** — Redacts JDBC, Postgres keyword DSN, SQL Server, and ODBC-style connection strings containing passwords.
37:6. **Bounded credential value detection** — Redacts password-like config values such as `DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED and `PGPASSWORD=REDACTED while preserving the surrounding key.
39:Detected secrets are replaced with `REDACTED` before the data is ever written to a git object. Of the six secret-detection passes above, the scanner layer (pass 2) is configurable — see [Choosing secret-scanner engines](#choosing-secret-scanner-engines) below — while the other five are **always on** and cannot be disabled. User-defined rules (inline `custom_redactions` and rule packs) add a seventh secret-detection pass that only runs when configured.
43:**Every layer described above — all nine passes, including the opt-in PII and OpenAI Privacy Filter layers — reads transcript *text*. There is no OCR pass, no vision-model PII or secret scan, and no gate that holds an image back until someone reviews it. Nothing in Entire ever reads what an image depicts.**

content.text:
I've read Entire's docs. It can do what the challenge wants, but **pushing a session record to your public repo has real risks**, so I'll set out the plan and wait for your go-ahead before installing anything.

## How it works
- `brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire`, then `entire enable --agent claude-code --import-history` in the repo. This installs git hooks and **imports existing Claude Code sessions from the last 30 days**, so our work so far can be included.
- On the next commit, Entire saves the session transcript as a checkpoint under `refs/entire/checkpoints/…` (not a branch) and adds an `Entire-Checkpoint:` line to the commit. Pushing sends the checkpoints to GitHub, which is what the challenge checks for.

## The risks
1. **Your two API keys are in this conversation in plain text.** Entire redacts secrets automatically, but its own docs call this "best-effort", and the repo is public. **Rotate both keys before anything is pushed**: OpenAI at platform.openai.com → API keys, ElevenLabs at elevenlabs.io → API keys. Then the old ones are useless even if a scan missed one.
   - **Don't paste the new keys into this chat.** Anything said in a session gets recorded. Enter them directly in the Vercel dashboard (Project → Settings → Environment Variables), or I'll give you a `vercel env add` command to type yourself.
2. **Screenshots are stored unredacted.** Entire saves pasted images as they are. Ours are screenshots of the app, your sketch and the board, so nothing sensitive, but they'll be public.
3. **It contradicts "don't mention Claude".** The record is a Claude Code session by definition, and commits get an `Entire-Checkpoint:` line. That's what the challenge requires, but it reverses your earlier rule.
4. **The whole conversation becomes public**, including our discussions about Vishwa's and Arjun's PRs.

content.content:
## Customizing redaction
The built-in detectors handle well-known secret formats. For anything else you don't want stored in transcripts — internal credential shapes the bundled scanners don't know about, project codenames, or specific words and phrases you'd rather keep out of session archives — Entire offers two extension surfaces. Both run plain regex matching against transcript content, so the rules can target any string pattern, not just credentials. Both feed the same engine and run as their own layer between connection-string detection and bounded credential KV detection.
### Surface 1: Inline `redaction.custom_redactions`
Add a label → regex map under `redaction.custom_redactions` in `.entire/settings.json`:
```json
{
  "redaction": {
    "custom_redactions": {
      "acme_token":  "ACME_TOKEN_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}",
      "internal_id": "INTERNAL_[a-z]{6}_[0-9]{4}"
    }
  }
}
```
- The label is for diagnostics only; matches are replaced with the bare `REDACTED` token (matching the built-in secret layers, not the `[REDACTED_<LABEL>]` token used for PII).
- Regexes follow [Go's RE2 syntax](https://pkg.go.dev/regexp/syntax). No lookarounds, no backreferences.
- A failed compile is logged once at startup and the rule is skipped — it will never crash the redactor.
- Override in `.entire/settings.local.json` for personal additions; entries merge per-key (override replaces the same key, leaves other keys intact).
### Surface 2: Rule packs
Drop a YAML or JSON file into `.entire/redactors/`:
```yaml
# .entire/redactors/acme-internal.yaml
name: acme-internal              # MUST match the filename stem
version: 1.0.0
description: Internal ACME service tokens
rules:
  - id: acme-token
    description: Long-lived ACME service tokens
    regex: 'ACME_TOKEN_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}'
    samples:
      - { input: "REDACTED", redacted: true  }
      - { input: "ACME_TOKEN_short",                     redacted: false }
  - id: acme-session
    regex: 'asess_[a-f0-9]{32}'
```
Equivalent JSON form:
```json
{
  "name": "acme-internal",
  "version": "1.0.0",

This file is a discovery stub, not the usage guide. Before running any `agent-browser` command, load the actual workflow content from the CLI:

The CLI serves skill content that always matches the installed version, so instructions never go stale. The content in this stub cannot change between releases, which is why it just points at `skills get core`.

## Specialized skills

Load a specialized skill when the task falls outside browser web pages:

```bash
agent-browser skills get electron          # Electron desktop apps (VS Code, Slack, Discord, Figma, ...)

## Why agent-browser

- Fast native Rust CLI, not a Node.js wrapper
- Works with any AI agent (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Continue, Windsurf, etc.)
- Chrome/Chromium via CDP with no Playwright or Puppeteer dependency
- Accessibility-tree snapshots with element refs for reliable interaction
- Sessions, authentication vault, state persistence, video recording
- Specialized skills for Electron apps, Slack, exploratory testing, cloud providers

## Observability Dashboard

The dashboard runs independently of browser sessions on port 4848 and can also be opened through a proxied or forwarded URL such as `https://dashboard.agent-browser.localhost`. Agents should stay on the dashboard origin: session tabs, status, and stream traffic are proxied internally, so session ports do not need to be exposed.

content.content:
---
name: core
description: Core agent-browser usage guide. Read this before running any agent-browser commands. Covers the snapshot-and-ref workflow, navigating pages, interacting with elements (click, fill, type, select), extracting text and data, taking screenshots, managing tabs, handling forms and auth, waiting for content, running multiple browser sessions in parallel, and troubleshooting common failures. Use when the user asks to interact with a website, fill a form, click something, extract data, take a screenshot, log into a site, test a web app, or automate any browser task.
allowed-tools: Bash(agent-browser:*), Bash(npx agent-browser:*)
---

# agent-browser core

Fast browser automation CLI for AI agents. Chrome/Chromium via CDP, no Playwright or Puppeteer dependency. Accessibility-tree snapshots with compact `@eN` refs let agents interact with pages in ~200-400 tokens instead of parsing raw HTML.

Most normal web tasks (navigate, read, click, fill, extract, screenshot) are covered here. Load a specialized skill when the task falls outside browser web pages — see [When to load another skill](#when-to-load-another-skill).

## The core loop

```bash
agent-browser open <url>        # 1. Open a page
agent-browser snapshot -i       # 2. See what's on it (interactive elements only)
agent-browser click @e3         # 3. Act on refs from the snapshot
agent-browser snapshot -i       # 4. Re-snapshot after any page change
```

Refs (`@e1`, `@e2`, ...) are assigned fresh on every snapshot. They become **stale the moment the page changes** — after clicks that navigate, form submits, dynamic re-renders, dialog opens. Always re-snapshot before your next ref interaction.

## Always use your own session

Before your first command, set a named session for the whole task:

```bash
export AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION="$(agent-browser session id --scope worktree --prefix task)"
```

The default (unnamed) session is a single shared browser: it is shared with every other agent on the machine and it persists across conversations, so working in it can hijack another agent's page mid-task or navigate away from something the human left open. Every example below assumes a named session is active. See [Run multiple browsers in parallel](#run-multiple-browsers-in-parallel) and `references/session-management.md`.

## Quickstart

```bash
# Install once
npm i -g agent-browser && agent-browser install

# Linux hosts can install required browser libraries too
agent-browser install --with-deps

# Take a screenshot of a page
agent-browser open https://example.com
agent-browser screenshot home.png
agent-browser close

# Search, click a result, and capture it
agent-browser open https://duckduckgo.com
agent-browser snapshot -i                      # find the search box ref
agent-browser fill @e1 "agent-browser cli"
agent-browser press Enter
agent-browser wait --load networkidle
agent-browser snapshot -i                      # refs now reflect results
agent-browser click @e5                        # click a result
agent-browser screenshot result.png
```

The browser stays running across commands so these feel like a single session. By default, an inactive daemon saves configured restore state, closes its headless browser, and exits after one hour; the next command starts it again. Without `--restore` or another restore key, shutdown discards transient browser state and open tabs. Dashboard mouse, keyboard, and touch input count as activity. Headed browsers, Safari and iOS WebDriver sessions, and user-attached browsers are exempt from the default; provider-owned cloud browsers are not. Use `--idle-timeout <time>` or `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` to tune the timeout, and use `0` to disable it. Still run `agent-browser close` (or `close --all`) when you're done.

## MCP integration

For tools that support Model Context Protocol servers, start the stdio server:

```bash
agent-browser mcp
agent-browser mcp --tools all
agent-browser mcp --tools core,network,react
```

Configure the MCP client to launch `agent-browser` with `["mcp"]`. The server defaults to MCP protocol 2025-11-25 and accepts older supported client protocol versions during initialization. The default tools profile is `core`, which keeps MCP context small for everyday browser automation. Use `--tools all` for the full typed CLI parity surface, or combine profiles with commas, such as `--tools core,network,react`. Profiles are `core`, `network`, `state`, `debug`, `tabs`, `react`, `mobile`, and `all`; the `debug` profile includes accessibility audits, plugin registry, and command.run tools. Each tool accepts typed arguments plus `extraArgs` for advanced CLI flags and exact CLI parity. # agent-browser core

Fast browser automation CLI for AI agents. Chrome/Chromium via CDP, no Playwright or Puppeteer dependency. Accessibility-tree snapshots with compact `@eN` refs let agents interact with pages in ~200-400 tokens instead of parsing raw HTML.

Most normal web tasks (navigate, read, click, fill, extract, screenshot) are covered here. Load a specialized skill when the task falls outside browser web pages — see [When to load another skill](#when-to-load-another-skill).

## The core loop

```bash
agent-browser open <url>        # 1. Open a page
agent-browser snapshot -i       # 2. See what's on it (interactive elements only)
agent-browser click @e3         # 3. Act on refs from the snapshot
agent-browser snapshot -i       # 4. Re-snapshot after any page change
```

Refs (`@e1`, `@e2`, ...) are assigned fresh on every snapshot. They become **stale the moment the page changes** — after clicks that navigate, form submits, dynamic re-renders, dialog opens. Always re-snapshot before your next ref interaction.

## Always use your own session

Before your first command, set a named session for the whole task:

```bash
export AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION="$(agent-browser session id --scope worktree --prefix task)"
```

The default (unnamed) session is a single shared browser: it is shared with every other agent on the machine and it persists across conversations, so working in it can hijack another agent's page mid-task or navigate away from something the human left open. Every example below assumes a named session is active. See [Run multiple browsers in parallel](#run-multiple-browsers-in-parallel) and `references/session-management.md`.

## Quickstart

```bash
# Install once
npm i -g agent-browser && agent-browser install

# Linux hosts can install required browser libraries too
agent-browser install --with-deps

# Take a screenshot of a page
agent-browser open https://example.com
agent-browser screenshot home.png
agent-browser close

# Search, click a result, and capture it
agent-browser open https://duckduckgo.com
agent-browser snapshot -i                      # find the search box ref
agent-browser fill @e1 "agent-browser cli"
agent-browser press Enter
agent-browser wait --load networkidle
agent-browser snapshot -i                      # refs now reflect results
agent-browser click @e5                        # click a result
agent-browser screenshot result.png
```

The browser stays running across commands so these feel like a single session. By default, an inactive daemon saves configured restore state, closes its headless browser, and exits after one hour; the next command starts it again. Without `--restore` or another restore key, shutdown discards transient browser state and open tabs. Dashboard mouse, keyboard, and touch input count as activity. content.content:
Create a repository and wait for provisioning to become active by
default. Active means provisioning completed; later pushes or mirror
creation can still fail for other reasons.

--wait-timeout must be positive. It bounds project resolution, creation,
and readiness polling after client setup, including creation with
--no-wait. Use --no-wait to return without confirming readiness.

If creation succeeds but readiness cannot be confirmed, the command exits
nonzero and preserves the repository result. Do not create again to
recover. With --json, stdout contains one repository object; progress
and recovery instructions go to stderr.

Usage:
  entire repo create <name> [flags]

Examples:
  entire repo create web --project acme
  entire repo create web --project acme --no-wait
  entire repo create web --project acme --wait-timeout=5m

Flags:
  -h, --help                    help for create
      --json                    Output raw JSON instead of a table
      --no-wait                 Return after creation without confirming provisioning readiness
      --object-format string    Git object format for the repository: sha1 or sha256 (defaults to the server default)
      --project string          Owning project (name or ULID) (required)
      --wait-timeout duration   Time limit for project resolution, creation, and provisioning readiness (default 10m0s)
